questions.q: What does a generator do differently from a list?
options: It makes values one at a time, when asked, instead of storing them all at once
questions.explain: In the lab, a million values took 8,448,728 bytes as a list and 200 bytes as a generator.

options: The function hands out a value and pauses; the next request carries on from there
The value is saved to a file
questions.explain: A generator remembers where it paused and all its local names, then resumes on the next next().

questions.q: You call order_numbers(), a function with yield in it. What runs?
options: Nothing yet: you get a generator object; the code runs when values are asked for
questions.explain: The yield_demo prints 'generator' first, and '(generator starts)' only after the first next().

questions.q: total = sum(amounts), then count = sum(1 for _ in amounts), where amounts is a generator. What is count?
options: 0: the first sum used the generator up, so the second loop finds nothing
An error on the second line
questions.explain: A generator can be used once. Do both jobs in one loop (the lab's fix).

questions.q: In paid_only(parse(read_lines(path))), when is the first line of the file read?
options: When the loop asks for the first paid order: then one line flows through all three steps
questions.explain: Building the pipeline reads nothing. Each request pulls one line through read → parse → filter.

questions.q: A @contextlib.contextmanager has try: yield / finally: close. An error happens inside the with block. Does the clean-up run?
options: Yes: finally runs even after an error, so the till always closes
Only if you catch the error
questions.explain: That's the point of context managers: with open(...) closes the file even if your code crashes halfway.

questions.q: (Going deeper) itertools.islice(read_lines(path), 3) on a 200,000-line file. How much of the file is read?
options: Only about the first 3 lines: the generator is never asked for more
questions.explain: Generators are lazy: nothing beyond what's asked for is ever produced.

questions.q: (Going deeper) In a context manager class, what does __exit__ returning True do?
options: Swallows the error, so it never reaches the caller: almost never what you want
questions.explain: Return False (or nothing) so errors still reach the caller after the clean-up.
